547.title: No closed fist
547.hook: the Buddha, ill, says there is no teacher's closed fist: nothing held back
547.carry: an open hand in both directions
547.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the open hand of DN 16 when they say there is no secret core held back for insiders, and Theravada communities chant and teach the suttas openly to anyone who comes.

segments.voice: Last time: Ambapali's invitation, and a promise kept to the one who asked first. Your line: first come, first honored. Today the rains come, and the Buddha falls ill.

The rains are about to begin. The Buddha sends the monks off to spend the season around Vesali, wherever they have friends, and stays on with Ananda in the little village of Beluva. Then the illness comes, sharp and dangerous. Ananda watches, frightened, and holds on to one hope. Surely the teacher won't go without some last word for the community. Something kept for the end, saved for the people closest to him.
screen: `THE RAINS AT BELUVA.` → `A SHARP ILLNESS.` → `WAITING FOR A LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: The sickness is severe. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says sharp pains came on him, close to death, and he bore them mindfully, without complaint. He thinks it wouldn't be right to pass away without speaking to the community, so he pushes the illness back by effort and recovers for a while. Then he sits in the shade, and Ananda comes and confesses how frightened he was. I took a little comfort, he says, in thinking you wouldn't go without leaving some instruction about the community. And the Buddha answers: what does the community expect of me, Ananda? I have taught the Dhamma without making any inside and outside. In the Pali, the Tathagata has no acariya-mutthi, no teacher's closed fist, holding something back for the end. Everything has already been given. Then he adds something just as surprising. He has never thought, I lead the community, or the community depends on me. So why would he need to leave instructions about leading it? And then, a picture of himself. I am old now, Ananda, eighty years old. Like an old cart kept going by being held together with straps, this body keeps going only by being held together. Two kinds of honesty in one scene. Nothing hidden about the teaching. Nothing hidden about the body either. The fist is open in both directions: here is everything I know, and here is how frail I am. A teacher could easily guard a secret, or a reputation. This one opens his hand.

548.title: Check it against the texts
548.hook: the four great references: test any claimed teaching against the discourses and the discipline
548.carry: set the words beside the discourses
548.howItsDone: Buddhist scholars and teachers still appeal to the four great references when weighing a disputed teaching, and different traditions define the body of texts used as the measure in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: acariyamutthi, and the Buddha's open hand at Beluva. Your line: an open hand in both directions. Today: if nothing is secret, how do you spot a fake?

A screenshot is going around. A famous quote, a soft background, a name underneath: the Buddha. Did he actually say it? Most people have no idea how to check, and the quote travels anyway. This is not a new problem. The Buddha knew that after he was gone people would say, I heard this from his own lips. So on the road north, at a town called Bhoganagara, he gave the monks a method. Four situations, one test.
screen: `A QUOTE WITH HIS NAME ON IT.` → `I HEARD IT FROM HIM.` → `A METHOD AT BHOGANAGARA.`

segments.voice: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta calls them the four great references, the mahapadesa. Suppose a monk says: I heard this from the Blessed One himself; this is the teaching, this is the discipline. Or: I heard it from a whole community, with its elders. Or: from a group of learned elders who know the texts by heart. Or: from one learned elder. Four sources, from the most impressive to the most modest. And the instruction is the same for all four. Don't welcome it, and don't scorn it. Learn the words carefully, then set them beside the discourses and compare them with the discipline. If they don't fit, conclude: this isn't the Buddha's word; this monk got it wrong. Set it aside. If they do fit, conclude: this is the Buddha's word; he got it right. Look at what the test doesn't care about. Not how famous the speaker is. Not how many people agree. Not even the claim, I heard it from him. The words themselves are checked against the body of teaching everyone can hear. It's yesterday's open hand, turned into a safeguard. Because nothing was secret, everything can be compared. Over the centuries, different Buddhist traditions have worked out which texts count as the measure, and they don't all draw that line in the same place. But the habit itself, check it against what's been taught, goes back to this road.

549.title: Four places
549.hook: the places of the birth, awakening, first sermon and passing, worth seeing with devotion
549.howItsDone: Buddhists from across Asia and the world make pilgrimage to Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar, often visiting all four on one journey, chanting, meditating and making offerings at each.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mahapadesa, the four great references. Your line: set the words beside the discourses. Today, a worry about the future, and four places on a map.

The Buddha is lying between the twin sal trees at Kusinara now, near the end. And Ananda raises a practical worry. Until now, he says, at the end of every rainy season, monks from all over came to see the Blessed One, and we got to see them, and learn from them. When you're gone, we won't have that. Where will people go? Underneath it sits a plainer question: where do we go now, to feel close? The Buddha's answer is very concrete.
screen: `BETWEEN THE SAL TREES.` → `WHERE WILL PEOPLE GO?` → `A CONCRETE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: There are four places, Ananda, that a person of faith should see, places that stir the heart. The Pali word is samvejaniya: stirring, moving. The first: here the Tathagata was born. The second: here the Tathagata awakened to full awakening. The third: here the Tathagata set the wheel of the Dhamma rolling. The fourth: here the Tathagata passed into final nibbana. The sutta itself doesn't name the towns. It simply says here, here, here, here. Tradition has filled in the map: Lumbini, in what is now Nepal; Bodh Gaya, under the tree; the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi, now called Sarnath; and Kusinara, where he is lying as he speaks. Then he adds that monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen, will come to these places, and whoever dies on such a pilgrimage with a heart at peace will be reborn in a good destination. It's a startling moment. A teacher who spent his life pointing people inward, to the breath and the mind, also says: go and stand there. The places don't hold magic in the text. They hold the four turning points of one life: arriving, waking up, sharing it, letting go. Pilgrims still travel between them.

550.title: Ananda weeps
550.hook: Ananda weeps outside; the Buddha praises him as the kindest attendant
550.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions honor Ananda as the disciple who remembered and recited the discourses, and the phrase 'thus have I heard' that opens many suttas is traditionally understood as his voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four places that stir the heart. Your line: places that stir the heart. Today the man who asked about those places slips away and cries.

Hospitals have a particular hallway. The one just outside the room, where family members go to fall apart for a minute so they can walk back in steady. Ananda has served the Buddha for many years: fetching water, guarding the door, keeping the teachings in memory. Now, at Kusinara, he goes into a dwelling, leans against the door frame, and weeps. I'm still a learner, he says. I still have work to do. And my teacher, who was so kind to me, is about to pass away. The Buddha notices he's gone and asks the monks: where is Ananda?
screen: `THE HALLWAY OUTSIDE THE ROOM.` → `LEANING ON THE DOOR FRAME.` → `WHERE IS ANANDA?`

segments.voice: He sends a monk: go and tell Ananda the teacher is calling him. Ananda comes back, bows, and sits to one side. The Buddha doesn't scold him. He says: enough, Ananda. Don't grieve, don't lament. Haven't I told you that we must be parted from everything dear to us? How could anything born, put together, bound to fall apart, not fall apart? Then he thanks him. For a long time, Ananda, you've attended on me with kindness in body, in speech and in mind, helpfully, gladly, wholeheartedly, without measure. You've done well. Keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Then he speaks to all the monks in praise of Ananda. The Buddhas of the past had attendants as good as Ananda, he says, and so will those of the future. Ananda is wise. He knows the right time for monks, nuns, lay followers, kings and teachers of other schools to come and see me. And he names something wonderful about him, true for monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen alike. When any of them come to see Ananda, they're glad just to see him. When he speaks, they're glad to hear him. And when he stops, they wish he'd go on. Later tradition says Ananda reached awakening the night before the first great council, where he recited the discourses. That, tradition says, is the voice behind their opening words: thus have I heard.

551.title: The teaching as teacher
551.hook: after I am gone, the dhamma and discipline will be your teacher
551.howItsDone: Theravada monastics treat the Dhamma and Vinaya as their teacher, reciting the monastic rules every fortnight, and many Buddhist schools also honor living lineages of teachers who pass the teaching on.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ananda in the doorway, comforted and praised. Your line: you've done well, Ananda. Today, the question every grieving student asks: who teaches us now?

A piano teacher dies. Her students still have the exercises she wrote in pencil on their sheet music, the habits she drilled into their hands, the sound of her voice saying slower. Do they have a teacher anymore? In one sense, no. In another, she's in every scale they play. The Buddha is lying between the sal trees, and before anyone asks, he names the question himself.
screen: `PENCIL MARKS ON THE SHEET MUSIC.` → `DO THEY STILL HAVE A TEACHER?` → `HE ANSWERS BEFORE IT'S ASKED.`

segments.voice: It may be, Ananda, he says, that some of you will think: the teacher's word is over; we have no teacher. Don't see it that way. The Dhamma and the discipline that I have taught and laid down for you, that will be your teacher when I am gone. In Pali the pair is dhamma-vinaya: the teaching, and the training rules that shape a community's life. Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't name a successor. He doesn't appoint a council. Earlier on this road he said he'd never thought of himself as the community's leader, and he stays consistent to the end. The teacher becomes something anyone can open. Then come a few practical instructions, and then a remarkable invitation. He asks the gathered monks: if any of you has a doubt or a question about the Buddha, the teaching, the community, the path or the practice, ask now. Don't regret later that you were face to face with the teacher and didn't ask. Silence. He asks a second time. Silence. A third time. Silence. Maybe you're holding back out of respect for me, he says; then tell a friend, and let the friend ask. Still silence. Ananda says it's wonderful: not one monk here has any doubt. A teacher who could have closed with a speech instead spends his last minutes asking three times, is anything unclear? If the teaching is going to be the teacher, it had better be understood.

552.title: Relics shared
552.hook: the passing, the cremation, and the relics divided among eight peoples
552.howItsDone: Buddhists across Asia honor relics of the Buddha and of great teachers in stupas and pagodas, walking around them clockwise, offering flowers and lights, and sitting nearby in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhamma-vinaya, and no successor named. Your line: the teaching is the teacher. Today the long story reaches its end, and then keeps going.

After a funeral, families sometimes fight over the strangest things. Not always the house. Sometimes a watch, a teapot, a box of letters. Anything that still feels like the person. When the Buddha dies at Kusinara, the same thing nearly happens on the scale of kingdoms. Seven peoples send messengers to the Mallas of Kusinara, each saying: he was one of us, too. We want a share of his remains. Tempers rise. And the one who stops a war is not a king, and not a monk.
screen: `WHAT STILL FEELS LIKE THEM.` → `SEVEN PEOPLES WANT A SHARE.` → `WHO STOPS THE WAR?`

segments.voice: First, the passing itself. After his question met silence three times, the Buddha speaks his last words to the monks: all conditioned things are subject to decay; strive on with heedfulness. Then he moves through the meditative absorptions, up and back down and up again, and passes away. The earth shakes. Some monks weep; others, the text says, bear it mindfully: everything put together comes apart. The Mallas honor the body for six days with music, dance and garlands. On the seventh they carry it to the pyre, but it won't catch fire until the elder Mahakassapa arrives with his monks and bows at the Buddha's feet. Then the pyre lights. Afterward, the bones remain. And the messengers come: King Ajatasattu, the Licchavis of Vesali, the Sakyans, the Bulis, the Koliyas, a brahmin of Vethadipa, the Mallas of Pava. The Mallas of Kusinara refuse: he died here. Then a brahmin named Dona speaks up. Our teacher, he reminds them, taught patience. It isn't right to fight over the remains of the best of men. Let's divide them into eight equal parts, so that shrines rise everywhere and many come to trust. Everyone agrees. Dona divides the relics, and asks only for the urn. The Moriyas arrive late and take the embers. Ten shrines rise, and the remains of the man who taught letting go are scattered, peacefully, across the land, and no one goes to war.

options: give them all to the most powerful king.
remind them he taught patience, and divide the relics into eight shares.
bury them where no one can find them.
fork.reveal: Dona says it isn't right to fight over the remains of one who taught patience, and divides them fairly.

original.note: Pali dhatu: element, and also a relic. the word for the remains Dona shared.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha's remains went to one great temple.
what it means: they were divided among eight peoples so no one would go to war, and shrines rose in many places.
what a scholar hears: DN 16 lists eight relic stupas plus the urn and embers stupas; the Piprahwa casket carries an inscription often read as referring to relics of the Buddha held by the Sakyas.

chat.says: What happened to the Buddha's remains after he died?
options: A brahmin, Dona, divided them among eight peoples so no one went to war.
They were all kept together in one great temple at Kusinara.
The kings went to war over them, and Ajatasattu won them all.
chat.meaning: Dona reminded everyone the Buddha taught patience and divided the relics into eight shares; with the urn and the embers, ten shrines rose.

553.title: All gone now
553.hook: a king's golden palaces and elephants, every one of them gone
553.carry: it was grand once, and it's gone
553.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Mahasudassana story to teach impermanence, and at funerals in Theravada countries monks chant the verse beginning 'anicca vata sankhara', impermanent indeed are conditioned things.

segments.voice: Yesterday: relics shared among eight peoples, and the Buddha's last words. Your line: strive on. Today closes a week, with a story the Buddha told about the little town where he died.

Kusinara was not much of a place. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Ananda pleads with the Buddha: please don't pass away in this little wattle-and-daub town, out in the jungle. There are great cities: Rajagaha, Savatthi, Varanasi. Go there. And the Buddha says: don't call it that, Ananda. Long ago, this was a royal city, and he begins to describe it. The seventeenth Long Discourse tells the whole story.
screen: `A LITTLE WATTLE-AND-DAUB TOWN.` → `DON'T CALL IT THAT.` → `ONCE A ROYAL CITY.`

segments.voice: The city was called Kusavati, and its king was Mahasudassana, the great and beautiful. The sutta lingers on every detail. Seven walls, of gold, silver, beryl, crystal and more. Rows of palm trees made of jewels, and when the wind moved their leaves, the sound was sweet and lovely, like a well-played orchestra, so that the people who heard it danced. Eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, eighty-four thousand elephants with golden trappings, chariots, horses, gems, and a whole court around him. The king was good, too. He gave freely, and in a palace built for him he sat alone and practiced, letting a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and calm fill every direction: the same practice as the trumpeter on day five hundred forty-two. And then the turn. Out of all those palaces, the king lived in only one. Out of all those elephants, he rode only one. And at the end, the Buddha tells Ananda: I was that king. And see, Ananda, all those things are past, ceased, changed. That is how impermanent conditioned things are. It's a strange kind of comfort. The Buddha is lying in a poor village, and he doesn't argue that it's secretly grand. He says it was grand once, and it's gone, as everything grand goes. Look back at this week: no closed fist, the four great references, the four places, Ananda in the doorway, the teaching as teacher, the relics shared, and now a golden city gone back to mud and thatch.
screen: `KUSAVATI, THE CITY OF JEWELS.` · `PALM TREES THAT MADE MUSIC.` · `HE LIVED IN ONLY ONE PALACE.` · `I WAS THAT KING.` · then, large: `ALL GONE NOW.`

segments.voice: Look at one fine thing near you, a cup you like, a plant, the light on a wall, kindly and fully, as if it's the best palace in the city. Then close your eyes and let yourself know it won't last forever, not with sadness, just with honesty. Keep the kindness and the honesty together, and breathe.
Anicca. The Mahasudassana Sutta's ending: a king's jeweled city, palaces and elephants, all past, ceased and changed. Today's word.
Your line: it was grand once, and it's gone. A fine thing is no less fine for passing. That closes the week.

fork.setup: Ananda begs you not to die in a humble jungle village. what do you, the Buddha, say?
options: agree, and set off for a great city.
tell him it was once a royal city, and that all its splendor has passed.
say that places don't matter at all.
fork.reveal: he tells the story of Kusavati and ends: all those things are past, ceased, changed.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. the lesson the Buddha draws from the vanished city.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kusinara was just a poor village.
what it means: in the Buddha's telling it was once Kusavati, a jeweled royal city, now all gone.
what a scholar hears: DN 17 expands a short passage in DN 16 into a full narrative and closes on impermanence; it is also a jataka-like story, with the Buddha naming himself as the king.

chat.says: Why did the dying Buddha tell Ananda about a jeweled city at Kusinara?
options: To show that everything grand passes: the city was splendid once, and it's gone.
To prove Kusinara was secretly still grand, so a fine place to die.
To say only great cities are worthy places for a Buddha to die.
chat.meaning: He says the humble village was once Kusavati, a jeweled royal city, and he was its king: all of it past, ceased, changed.

Kusavati.meaning: the jeweled royal city that Kusinara once was
